abstract: Parasite fitness is often constrained by the transmission-virulence trade-off, where excessive replication within a host shortens infection duration and reduces overall transmission. Spatial structure has been shown to influence selection acting on this evolutionary trade-off: limited parasite dispersal shapes how transmission affects fitness and alters population genetic structure. However, while current theory assumes that parasite dispersal is fixed and independent of virulence, parasites typically modulate host mobility, a sublethal effect that has a direct impact on the spatial structure of populations. Here, we expand the classical virulence-transmission trade-off framework by considering the impact of virulence on host mobility. We find that when parasites reduce host movement, relatedness and local demographic conditions change in ways that favour more prudent parasite strategies that inflict less harm. Furthermore, while parasite-impaired host mobility leads to higher host density, long-lived hosts also shed parasites for longer periods leading to increased parasite prevalence across the population. We further show that such population-level demographic feedbacks are crucial for clarifying previous results on why limited parasite dispersal reduces virulence. Our work highlights the importance of incorporating host behaviour in models of parasite virulence and suggests new avenues for managing infectious disease in natural populations.

summary: Theoretical model showing parasite-impaired host mobility reduces parasite virulence via altered relatedness and host density, with feedbacks on prevalence.
title: Parasite impairment of host mobility favours reduced virulence.
